query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack-aluminizing treatment at 900–1000 °C in an inert atmosphere to form a continuous, adherent Al-rich oxide scale on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly reduce oxygen ingress at 800–1000 °C in air for at least 5 hours under strain rates up to 10⁻² s⁻¹, preserving or improving the alloy’s high-temperature mechanical properties compared to untreated material.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy in the as-cast condition.
generation.intervention: Pack-aluminization at 900–1000 °C for several hours in argon to diffuse aluminum into the near-surface region.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature service in air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 hours with strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, low-diffusivity alumina-based surface oxide layer that impedes oxygen penetration.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum introduced via pack-cementation reacts with oxygen to form a stable, adherent Al-rich oxide scale that slows oxidation kinetics, thereby limiting oxygen ingress and preventing rapid embrittlement while maintaining high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the coated alloy will exhibit significantly reduced mass gain, less oxide spallation, and retention of tensile strength and ductility following 5-hour exposure in air at 800–1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr tested without any protective coating under equivalent high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected for short-to-medium-term exposures (e.g., up to 5 hours) in air, at 800–1000 °C, with strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹. Performance for longer exposures and more aggressive environments remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Potential variation in Al diffusion depth or formation of unwanted brittle phases at the interface could limit ductility, and the long-term stability of the coating at temperatures above 1000 °C remains unverified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens. Subject one set to pack-aluminizing at 900–1000 °C for several hours in argon and leave the other set uncoated. Expose both sets to 800–1000 °C in air for 5 hours. Subsequently, measure mass gain, examine oxide scale adherence, and perform tensile testing at both room temperature and high temperature (e.g., 1000 °C).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a measurable reduction in mass gain or if they exhibit comparable or worse mechanical performance to the uncoated samples after exposure, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. decision.trend: Initial studies on near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr have focused on arc-cast processing and post-treatment to improve mechanical performance at high temperatures (PMC5578249) but did not address oxidation resistance directly. Parallel work on other refractory alloys (PMC5995863) achieved improved high-temperature strength and some oxidation protection by forming protective compounds (e.g., in situ ceramics). However, a robust, scalable method to protect cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr from oxygen ingress without sacrificing mechanical properties remains unproven.
decision.unsolved: No prior investigation has clearly demonstrated an effective way to form a stable, slow-growing oxide or diffusion barrier on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. Methods that worked for related alloys have not been validated on this exact composition, leaving open the question of whether a facile surface engineering or thermochemical approach can yield the required oxidation resistance at 800–1000 °C in air while preserving strength and ductility.
decision.lever: A pack-aluminizing treatment at ~900–1000 °C for several hours in an argon atmosphere to form a continuous, adherent, protective Al-rich oxide scale on the cast alloy surface.
decision.why: Studies on other refractory alloys showed improved oxidation resistance from stable oxide or ceramic scales. Since alloying additions are not allowed, forming an aluminide-type coating via pack cementation leverages external diffusion of Al to the surface without altering bulk composition. The dense oxide layer should hinder oxygen penetration and preserve bulk mechanical properties under typical service conditions (5+ hours in air, 800–1000 °C, up to strain rates of 10−2 s−1). A controlled experiment exposing coated versus uncoated samples at 800–1000 °C in air for 5 h, then evaluating oxygen ingress (e.g., via microscopy and mass gain), would falsify the hypothesis if the coated samples fail to show significantly reduced oxidation compared to the untreated material.
